bp: A large video site has to decide, many times a day, which few videos should appear in front of a person. The easy goal is watch time: show the videos the person is most likely to keep watching. But a platform is also an ecosystem. If the same familiar channels, creators, or content types keep winning, viewers receive less variety and emerging creators receive fewer chances to be discovered. This paper studies that pressure at the final ordering stage of video recommendation. The target is familiarity bias: the tendency for known content to dominate because the user already has a history with it. The paper's practical aim is not to replace the whole recommender. It tries to make the final ranked list less trapped by familiarity while still preserving the platform goals the abstract names: stable overall watch time, short-term satisfaction, creator exposure, and content diversity.
wh: The hard part is that familiar content is not simply bad. A viewer may genuinely enjoy a creator they already know, and a recommendation system should not punish that preference blindly. The problem is that familiarity can become extra evidence on top of preference. Past exposure creates more interactions, more ratings, and more confidence, so the ranking system may learn that known content is safer even when a less familiar video could also satisfy the viewer. That creates a loop: familiar items are shown because they have evidence, and they gain more evidence because they are shown. Novel content and emerging creators stay uncertain because they receive fewer chances. A fix also has to run inside a real serving stack, after other ranking work has already happened. It must be lightweight, work with existing models, and avoid damaging the watch time and satisfaction measures that keep the product usable.
naive: A smart beginner might reserve a fixed share of every recommendation list for unfamiliar videos, or subtract the same penalty from every video the user has seen before. That fails because users do not have the same relationship to familiarity. One viewer may repeatedly return to a known creator for good reasons; another may be stuck seeing known material because the system rarely offers alternatives. A flat novelty quota can push weak candidates into the list and hurt satisfaction. A flat penalty can remove videos that are both familiar and genuinely wanted. The abstract says LAFB instead estimates personalized debiasing factors, which means the correction changes with the user and the content rather than treating all familiarity as the same mistake.
ap: The central move is to treat familiarity as a measurable pressure in the final ranking, then adjust predicted rating scores by a personalized correction. LAFB, or Learning to Alleviate Familiarity Bias, sits in the post-ranking stage. That means another recommender has already produced candidate videos and predicted how much the user may value them. LAFB does not need to be the main ranking model. It models how familiar a user is with content using both discrete interaction features, such as count-like or category-like signs of prior interaction, and continuous interaction features, such as graded amounts of exposure or engagement. From those features it estimates debiasing factors for that particular user-content pair. The adjusted score then changes the final ordering, reducing the automatic dominance of familiar content while still letting strong familiar recommendations remain when the evidence supports them.
mech: The mechanism can be read as a late-stage score repair process. First, the serving system has a set of candidate videos for a user and a predicted rating score for each candidate. That score stands in for expected usefulness under the platform's existing recommendation model. Second, LAFB builds a description of user-content familiarity. The abstract says this description uses discrete and continuous interaction features, so the input is not just a yes-or-no flag for whether the user has seen something like this before. It can represent different shapes and degrees of previous interaction. Third, the method learns a personalized debiasing factor from those familiarity signals. In plain terms, it asks how much of the current score may be inflated by the safety and evidence advantage of familiar material for this user. Fourth, the method applies that factor to the predicted rating score, producing an adjusted score. Fifth, the final list is sorted from these adjusted scores. The output is still a ranked video list, but the list has less pressure toward already familiar content. The abstract reports two kinds of evaluation: large-scale offline tests and online A/B testing inside a real recommendation system. It also says the serving stack compared LAFB with deployable popularity-oriented remedies, which matters because the method was tested against alternatives that could actually run in production.
math: The main mathematical object is a score used for ranking. A score compresses many signs about a user and a video into one number so videos can be ordered. The danger is that the number can mix true preference with exposure history. LAFB adds a second mathematical object: a learned correction factor. A factor is a multiplier or adjustment that changes a score without replacing the entire scoring system. The correction is personalized, so it is closer to estimating a local bias for this user-content pair than applying a global rule. The paper also uses feature-based learning. Features are measured clues: some are discrete, meaning they fall into separate buckets or counts; others are continuous, meaning they vary by degree. Learning here means using past interaction evidence to choose how those clues should change the debiasing factor. The ranking idea is then constrained comparison: videos are still compared by scores, but the scores are altered so familiarity does not count as strongly when it mainly reflects prior exposure. The tradeoff is engagement versus discovery, with short-term satisfaction and watch time on one side and novel watch-time share, emerging creator exposure, and content diversity on the other. The math fits because the product decision is comparative and late-stage: a small score adjustment can change which borderline videos become visible.
dots: This paper sits where recommendation, ranking, fairness, and probability meet. It is a recommender paper because the object is a user choosing among videos. It is a ranking paper because the final decision is an ordered list, and small changes near the visible cutoff matter. It is a fairness and bias paper because exposure is uneven: emerging creators and less familiar content can lose attention even when they might be valuable. It also has a probability flavor because the original rating prediction is an estimate under uncertainty, and familiarity can make that estimate look safer than it really is. In the repo's broader recommendation family, this is one branch of the shared problem of repairing comparison before selection. Other recommender papers may address missing modalities, long behavior histories, cold starts, or time-aware transfer. LAFB addresses a different surface symptom: the system has too much confidence in what the user already knows.
ww: The method should help because it attacks the loop at the place where the loop becomes visible: the final order. Familiar content often has many prior interactions, so the main recommender can treat it as a lower-risk choice. If LAFB can estimate when that advantage is partly familiarity rather than actual added preference, then reducing the score slightly can let nearby unfamiliar candidates rise. This does not require forcing random novelty into the list. It only changes comparisons where the learned factor says familiarity is distorting the score. Personalization is important because the same amount of prior interaction can mean different things for different people. For one viewer, repeated watching may show a stable preference. For another, it may show that the system has narrowed the menu. Running after the main ranking stage also makes the idea deployable: it can adjust outputs from existing models, compare against other post-ranking remedies, and preserve the serving stack. The abstract's online A/B testing and YouTube launch are evidence that the adjustment was practical enough for real traffic, not only an offline score exercise.
po: The payoff is a recommender that can make room for discovery without throwing away engagement. The abstract says LAFB increases novel watch-time share, improves exposure for emerging creators, and improves overall content diversity. It also says overall watch time and short-term satisfaction remain stable. That combination is the important result: the method buys a way to reduce familiar-content dominance in the final ranking while keeping the system acceptable to viewers and the platform. The YouTube launch strengthens the practical claim, because it shows the method fit an existing large-scale recommendation pipeline.
limits: The abstract does not prove that familiarity is always harmful, only that reducing its dominance improved the reported measures in this setting. The method assumes that interaction features can separate useful familiarity from biased overexposure well enough to guide score adjustment. It also assumes the original predicted rating scores are worth repairing rather than replacing. The reported benefits depend on the chosen metrics: novel watch-time share, emerging creator exposure, diversity, overall watch time, and short-term satisfaction. The abstract does not show long-term user welfare, creator outcomes beyond exposure, effects across all creator groups, or whether the same factors transfer to platforms unlike YouTube.
